848.title: Rufaydah al-Aslamiyyah
848.hook: who kept a tent to treat the wounded, remembered by some as a first nurse
848.howItsDone: Muslims remember Rufaydah from the early biography of the Prophet, where her tent in the mosque at Medina is where the wounded were cared for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asma bint Abi Bakr, who cut her belt in two and held up the name in front of a governor. Your line was: she of the two belts. Did anyone bring up your past today? Day eight hundred forty-eight.

Sahih al-Bukhari mentions a tent set up in the mosque at Medina, so that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, could look in on a wounded man from close by. It does not say whose tent it was. A wounded man had been carried in from the fighting, and someone had to stop the bleeding, change the dressings, sit through the night. Another early source gives that someone a name, in just a few lines. Today: Rufaydah, from the tribe of Aslam.
screen: `A CLOTH PRESSED TO A WOUND.` → `A TENT BY THE MOSQUE.` → `A NAME IN A FEW LINES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the sources keep. The wounded man in Bukhari's report is Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, hit at the battle of the Trench. Bukhari doesn't name who ran the tent. The early biography of the Prophet by Ibn Ishaq fills that in: the tent belonged to a woman of Aslam named Rufaydah, who treated the wounded, and who gave her own effort to caring for Muslims in need. That's nearly all. No speeches. No long story. A woman, a tent, and wounds that needed looking after. She wasn't the only woman doing this work. Bukhari also keeps the words of al-Rubayyi bint Mu'awwidh, who said that the women went out with the Prophet, gave water to the fighters, served them, and carried the wounded and the dead back to Medina. So Rufaydah stands in a line of women who did the unglamorous part. Notice where her tent was. Not at the edge of town. In the mosque, the center of the community, right where people prayed. Healing was given a place beside worship, not behind it. Some today call Rufaydah the first nurse of Islam. The old reports say something smaller: she treated the wounded, and the Prophet sent a wounded leader to her. The tent of healing. The sources never describe the tent itself. They keep who was lying in it, and whose it was.
screen: `A TENT IN THE MOSQUE FOR SA'D.` · `IBN ISHAQ: IT WAS RUFAYDAH'S.` · `WOMEN CARRIED THE WOUNDED HOME.` · `HEALING BESIDE WORSHIP.` · then, large: `THE TENT OF HEALING.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a nurse. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has cared for a body you love. A nurse in a hospital, a midwife, a carer at a home, a parent up at three in the morning with a fever. Maybe it was you. See their hands. Breathe in, and hold them in your attention. Breathe out, and let a plain thank you form. Then choose: can you say it to them, or write it? If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for those who tend the sick. The bell holds the time.
Rufaydah al-Aslamiyyah. The woman of Aslam whose tent in Medina was where the wounded were treated. Today's word.
Your line: the tent of healing. Today, thank one nurse or carer by name, in person, by message, or on a card. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: Al-Shifa bint Abdullah
849.hook: who taught writing and, reports say, oversaw the market
849.howItsDone: Muslims remember al-Shifa from a report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, where the Prophet asks her to teach Hafsah a healing charm as she had taught her writing; later biographical works add that she had a role in the market.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rufaydah, the woman of Aslam who tended the wounded by the mosque. Your line was: the tent of healing. Which nurse or carer did you thank? Day eight hundred forty-nine.

Who taught the Prophet's wife to write? The answer turns up in an unlikely place, a chapter of hadith about medicine and charms. A room in Medina. Hafsah, one of the wives of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is sitting with a woman named al-Shifa. The Prophet walks in, sees them together, and says something that only makes sense if everyone in the room already knows a small fact. Today: al-Shifa, daughter of Abdullah, and the fact the Prophet took for granted.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT HAFSAH TO WRITE?` → `TWO WOMEN IN A ROOM.` → `THE PROPHET WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by al-Shifa herself. She was with Hafsah when the Prophet came in, and he said to her: won't you teach her the charm for skin sores, as you taught her writing? That's all. One sentence. But look at what it holds. Al-Shifa knew a healing recitation, the kind people said over a painful rash, and the Prophet asked her to pass it on. And in the same breath, almost in passing, he mentions that she had already taught Hafsah to write. He doesn't praise it as unusual. He uses it as the model: do this the way you did that. A woman teaching a woman to write, in the Prophet's own household, and his response is: good, now teach her this too. Her name, al-Shifa, is the Arabic word for healing, which fits the charm. But the line that lasts is the other one. She taught writing. Later reports, in biographical works compiled long after, say that the caliph Umar gave her a role in the market of Medina, keeping an eye on trade. Some scholars accept those reports, and some doubt them, and the details differ. So hold that part lightly. The part that's firm is the room with Hafsah, and a teacher whose teaching the Prophet simply assumed. There is something very ordinary about it. No speech about learning. No ceremony. Just one person who could write, sitting with one person who couldn't yet, until she could.
screen: `TEACH HER THE CHARM FOR SORES.` · `AS YOU TAUGHT HER WRITING.` · `THE MARKET: REPORTS DIFFER.` · `ONE PERSON TEACHING ONE PERSON.` · then, large: `SHE TAUGHT WRITING.`

segments.voice: The practice: teach someone to read something. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind who first taught you letters. A parent's finger under a word, a teacher, an older sibling. Breathe in, and remember the page. Breathe out, and thank them in your heart. Now look around your life for someone who could use a reader beside them. A child sounding out a sign. A parent with a confusing form. A friend learning a new script, or a new language. Choose one thing you could help them read this week. If you pray, you can ask for patience to teach well. The bell holds the time.
Al-Shifa bint Abdullah. A woman of Mecca and Medina whom the Prophet asked to teach a healing charm, as she had taught Hafsah to write. Today's word.
Your line: she taught writing. Today, sit beside one person and help them read one thing, slowly, all the way through. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: Umm Sulaym
850.hook: who accepted faith as her dowry, and bore a grief with remarkable patience (Bukhari)
850.howItsDone: Muslims tell Umm Sulaym's story from al-Nasa'i, where her dowry is Abu Talhah's Islam, and from Bukhari and Muslim, where she breaks the news of their son's death; at a loss, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Shifa bint Abdullah, who taught Hafsah to write. Your line was: she taught writing. Who did you sit beside while they read? Day eight hundred fifty.

A man of Medina named Abu Talhah comes to ask a woman to marry him. The woman is Umm Sulaym, the mother of Anas, the boy who served the Prophet, whom we met earlier on this road. She has become Muslim. He has not. When the talk turns to a dowry, she names one, and it isn't anything he can carry in his hands. Today: Umm Sulaym, in two scenes, one at the start of a marriage and one in the middle of it.
screen: `A PROPOSAL IN MEDINA.` → `NOT GOLD.` → `TWO SCENES IN ONE MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: The first scene is in the Sunan of al-Nasa'i. Abu Talhah proposed, and Umm Sulaym answered that a man like him was not someone to turn away, but she was a Muslim and he was not, and she could not marry him as things were. If you accept Islam, she said, that will be my dowry, and I'll ask you for nothing else. He accepted Islam, and that was her dowry. Faith for a dowry. The second scene is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and it is hard. Their young son was ill, and while Abu Talhah was out, the boy died. Umm Sulaym prepared the child, laid him aside, and told the household not to tell his father until she did. When Abu Talhah came home and asked about the boy, she said he was calmer than he had been, and she hoped he was at rest. She brought him his supper. They spent the night together. In the morning, she told him. Sahih Muslim's version adds how she told him: she asked, if people lent something to a family and then asked for it back, would the family have the right to refuse? No, he said. Then, she said, seek your reward from God for your son. He went to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and told him everything. The Prophet prayed for blessing on their night together. Readers take this story in different ways. Some see astonishing patience. Some find it hard to read. Both reactions sit honestly with it. What is clear is that Umm Sulaym chose her moment. She let her husband eat and rest before she gave him the news, and she gave it to him in a picture he could hold. A loan, returned.
screen: `IF YOU ACCEPT ISLAM, THAT IS MY DOWRY.` · `THE BOY DIED WHILE HE WAS OUT.` · `HE IS CALMER; I HOPE HE IS AT REST.` · `A LOAN, RETURNED.` · then, large: `FAITH FOR A DOWRY.`

segments.voice: The practice: hold one hard thing gracefully. This one can be gentle. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one hard thing you're carrying right now. Not the hardest. One you can look at. Hold it the way you'd hold something fragile. Breathe in around it. Breathe out, and don't push it away. Ask one question: is there a better moment, or a kinder way, to say what needs saying about it? If you pray, you can say what Muslims say at a loss: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, to God we belong and to Him we return. The bell holds the time.
Umm Sulaym. The mother of Anas, who asked for Islam as her dowry and told her husband of their son's death in a picture of a loan returned. Today's word.
Your line: faith for a dowry. Today, when you have hard news to give, choose the moment and the words with care. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: Hassan ibn Thabit
851.hook: the poet of the Prophet ﷺ, who defended him in verse
851.howItsDone: Muslims remember Hassan ibn Thabit as the poet of the Prophet, from reports in Bukhari and in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi that a pulpit was set up for him in the mosque, and some Muslims still recite poems in praise of the Prophet today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Sulaym, who asked for Islam as her dowry and told hard news as a loan returned. Your line was: faith for a dowry. When did you choose your moment with care? Day eight hundred fifty-one.

Lines of verse mocking the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, are being passed from mouth to mouth. Not arrows. Rhymes. A sharp line is easy to remember, and it can make a man look like a fool to people who have never met him. So what does a community do when it's being attacked in verse? Ignore it? Answer with force? Or find a poet of its own. Today: Hassan ibn Thabit, who answered.
screen: `VERSES MOCKING THE PROPHET.` → `NOT ARROWS. RHYMES.` → `WHO WOULD ANSWER?`

segments.voice: Hassan was a man of Medina and a poet. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the Prophet's charge to him. In one report, the Prophet tells Hassan to answer the poets who were mocking, and says that Gabriel is with him. In another, the Prophet's words are: answer on my behalf, and he prays, O God, support him with the Holy Spirit. A poet, told that his verses had help from heaven. Then there's the pulpit. Aisha reports, in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, that the Prophet had a pulpit set up for Hassan in the mosque. Hassan would stand on it and defend the Prophet in verse. The poet's pulpit. Poetry, in the place of prayer, on a raised step, with permission. Not everyone was comfortable with that. Bukhari tells a scene after the Prophet's death. Umar passes Hassan reciting in the mosque and shows his disapproval. Hassan doesn't back down. I used to recite in here, he says, when someone better than you was present. Then he turns to Abu Hurayrah and asks him, by God, whether he heard the Prophet say: answer on my behalf, O God, support him with the Holy Spirit. Abu Hurayrah says yes. So Hassan's art was a kind of service. He took the weapon that was being used against the community and turned it into a defense. And he did it with the Prophet's blessing, standing in the mosque, in the open. Words can wound. Hassan's answer was more words, placed where everyone could hear.
screen: `ANSWER ON MY BEHALF.` · `SUPPORT HIM WITH THE HOLY SPIRIT.` · `A PULPIT IN THE MOSQUE.` · `UMAR FROWNS; HASSAN STANDS FIRM.` · then, large: `THE POET'S PULPIT.`

segments.voice: The practice: four lines in praise. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone or something that deserves defending or honoring. A friend who's being talked about unfairly. A teacher. A place you love. If you pray, it can be praise of God. Breathe in, and find the first line. It doesn't need to rhyme. Breathe out, and find the second. Keep going, slowly, until there are four. Short lines are fine. True lines are better than clever ones. Hold them in your head until the bell, then write them down. The bell holds the time.
Hassan ibn Thabit. The poet of Medina who answered the Prophet's critics in verse, from a pulpit in the mosque. Today's word.
Your line: the poet's pulpit. Today, send your four lines of praise to the person they're about, or read them out to someone. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

852.title: Ka'b ibn Malik
852.hook: one of the three who stayed behind from Tabuk and refused to lie (Bukhari)
852.howItsDone: Muslims tell Ka'b ibn Malik's story from his own long account in Sahih al-Bukhari, read alongside surah 9:118, as a lesson in truthfulness and repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hassan ibn Thabit, who answered the Prophet's critics in verse. Your line was: the poet's pulpit. Did your four lines reach the one they were about? Day eight hundred fifty-two.

The army has come home, and one by one, the men who stayed behind file in to explain themselves. Each one has a reason, and swears to it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, listens, accepts what they say, and asks God to forgive them. Then it's Ka'b's turn. He's a good talker. He knows it. He could build an excuse in his sleep. And he has no excuse at all. He simply put off getting ready, day after day, until the army was gone. Today: Ka'b ibn Malik, and the story he tells against himself.
screen: `THE MEN WHO STAYED BEHIND.` → `ONE EXCUSE AFTER ANOTHER.` → `KA'B HAS NONE.`

segments.voice: Ka'b tells this himself, in a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari. Before the Tabuk expedition, he says, he had never been stronger or better off. He kept meaning to prepare, and kept not doing it. Then the army left. When the Prophet returned, Ka'b came before him, and the Prophet smiled the smile of someone who is angry. Ka'b says he knew he could talk his way out of anyone's anger. But if I lie to you today, he told the Prophet, you may be pleased with me now, and God will soon turn you against me. If I tell you the truth, you'll be angry, and I hope for God's forgiveness. I had no excuse. The Prophet said: as for this one, he has told the truth. Go, until God decides about you. Then came the hard part. People were told not to speak to Ka'b and to the two others who had owned up. Ka'b would greet the Prophet and wonder whether his lips moved to answer. His own cousin would not reply to him. A letter arrived from a foreign king inviting him to come over, and Ka'b threw it in the oven. Fifty nights, the report says, the earth felt narrow to him. Then the Qur'an spoke of the three who were left behind, and of God turning to them in mercy, in surah nine. A man climbed a hill and shouted the good news. Ka'b's conclusion is the line he chose to be remembered by. God saved me only through truthfulness, he said, and part of my repentance is to speak nothing but the truth as long as I live. Truth saved him. Not quickly. Not comfortably. But it did.
screen: `I HAD NO EXCUSE.` · `AS FOR THIS ONE, HE HAS TOLD THE TRUTH.` · `NO ONE WOULD SPEAK TO HIM.` · `GOD TURNED TO THE THREE.` · then, large: `TRUTH SAVED HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: the truth that costs. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you've been explaining away? A late reply with a made-up reason. A mistake you let someone else carry. A small cover story. Find one. Breathe in, and say to yourself, plainly, what actually happened. No excuse attached. Breathe out, and notice how that sits in your body. Then picture saying it to the person it concerns, in one or two sentences. If you pray, you can ask God for the courage of Ka'b. The bell holds the time.
Ka'b ibn Malik. One of the three who stayed behind from Tabuk, refused to make an excuse, and was forgiven through the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: truth saved him. Today, tell one small truth that costs you something, with no excuse attached. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

853.title: Suhayb the Roman
853.hook: who gave all his wealth to be allowed to emigrate, and was told, the trade was profitable (sirah)
853.howItsDone: Muslims tell Suhayb's story from the early biographies of the Prophet, and some commentators read it alongside surah 2:207, about one who sells himself seeking God's pleasure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ka'b ibn Malik, who had no excuse and said so. Your line was: truth saved him. What small truth did you tell that cost you something? Day eight hundred fifty-three.

The road out of Mecca is blocked. A man is trying to leave for Medina, where the Prophet and his companions have gone, and some men of Quraysh stand in his way. They have a point to make, and it's about money. You came here with nothing, they tell him. You got rich among us. And now you want to walk off with all of it? Not a chance. He could argue. He could fight. He could turn back and wait for a better day. Instead he asks them a question. Today: Suhayb, called the Roman.
screen: `THE ROAD OUT IS BLOCKED.` → `YOU GOT RICH AMONG US.` → `HE ASKS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the early biographies of the Prophet. Suhayb's question to the men on the road was simple. If I give you my wealth, will you let me go? They said yes. So he told them where it was, handed it over, and left for Medina with nothing. When word of it reached the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, he said, as the biographies tell it: Suhayb has profited. Suhayb has profited. Why the Roman? Tradition says Suhayb was an Arab by birth who was carried off as a child and grew up among the Byzantines, the Romans of that time, until his speech carried their accent, and later came to Mecca, where he made his living as a trader. So he knew exactly what money was, and what a deal was. That's what makes the Prophet's words land. He didn't say Suhayb was generous, or brave. He spoke a trader's language back to a trader. You've made a profit. Some commentators on the Qur'an connect Suhayb to a verse in surah two about a person who sells his own self, seeking the good pleasure of God. Not every commentator links the verse to him, and the verse speaks for itself either way. But the picture is the same. Everything on one side of the scale. On the other, the road to where he wanted to be. A roadblock like that may never come. The question can still come in small sizes. What would you give up, to go where you want to go? A comfort, a habit, an evening. The trade the Prophet praised was not a loss dressed up as virtue. He called it a profit.
screen: `IF I GIVE YOU MY WEALTH, WILL YOU LET ME GO?` · `SUHAYB HAS PROFITED.` · `A TRADER'S WORD TO A TRADER.` · `ONE WHO SELLS HIS OWN SELF.` · then, large: `A PROFITABLE TRADE.`

segments.voice: The practice: trade a comfort for a good. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small comfort that's been standing between you and something good. An extra hour of scrolling that could be a call to your mother. A takeout order that could be a gift to someone who needs it. A lie-in that could be a dawn prayer, if you pray, or a walk. Breathe in, and hold both sides of the trade. Breathe out, and choose one. Don't make it big. Make it real. The bell holds the time.
Suhayb the Roman. The trader who handed over his wealth to be let go to Medina, and was told by the Prophet that he had profited. Today's word.
Your line: a profitable trade. Today, make the trade you chose, one comfort given up for one good done. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

854.title: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt
854.hook: a blacksmith who suffered for his faith in Mecca, and lived to see the community grow
854.howItsDone: Muslims tell Khabbab's story from his own reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, where he speaks of his trade, of asking the Prophet for help in Mecca, and of the companions who did and did not live to see the community grow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suhayb the Roman, who handed over his wealth at a roadblock and was told he had profited. Your line was: a profitable trade. What comfort did you trade, and for what? Day eight hundred fifty-four.

I won't pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad. A man in Mecca says that to the craftsman he owes. The craftsman is a blacksmith named Khabbab, come to collect for work already done. The man who owes him is al-As ibn Wa'il. The bill is real: the work is done, and the money is owed. The price he puts on paying it is Khabbab's faith. Today: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, the blacksmith.
screen: `AN ANVIL AND A FIRE.` → `AN UNPAID BILL.` → `A PRICE FOR HIS FAITH.`

segments.voice: That scene is Khabbab's own telling, in Sahih al-Bukhari. He says he was a blacksmith, and he answered al-As that he would not disbelieve, not until al-As died and was raised again. Bukhari connects verses in surah nineteen to that exchange. Tradition says Khabbab paid for his faith with his body too, that he was made to lie on hot coals, and that years later he showed the scars on his back. The texts keep something quieter as well. In another report in Bukhari, Khabbab remembers going to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who was resting on his cloak in the shade of the Kaaba. Won't you ask God to help us? he asked. The Prophet sat up. He spoke of believers before them who had suffered terribly and still not turned from their faith. Then he said God would complete this matter, until a rider could travel from San'a to Hadramawt fearing no one but God, and the wolf for his sheep. But you are in a hurry, he said. That's a hard answer to hear when you are the one who is hurting. It doesn't deny the pain. It widens the frame. And Khabbab did live to see the frame widen. A third report in Bukhari has him, much later, remembering the companions who emigrated. Some of them died before tasting any reward, he says, and he names Mus'ab ibn Umayr, whom we have met on this road. And some of us, Khabbab says, have seen our fruit ripen, and we are picking it. The blacksmith endured. In his own reports, what he holds on to is not that the fire was small, but the wider frame the Prophet showed him.
screen: `NOT UNTIL YOU DIE AND RISE AGAIN.` · `WON'T YOU ASK GOD TO HELP US?` · `A RIDER WHO FEARS NO ONE BUT GOD.` · `OUR FRUIT HAS RIPENED.` · then, large: `THE BLACKSMITH ENDURED.`

segments.voice: This week ran from Rufaydah's tent, through al-Shifa, Umm Sulaym, Hassan, Ka'b and Suhayb, to Khabbab. The practice: endure a small discomfort for good. Sit up straight, a little straighter than is easy, and stay there. Breathe. Let your shoulders feel it. This is not suffering, just a small, chosen effort. Breathe in, and name one good thing this discomfort could stand for: someone you're helping, something you're building. Breathe out, and stay. If you pray, you can ask God for patience. The bell holds the time.
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt. The blacksmith of Mecca who would not give up his faith for an unpaid debt, and lived to see the fruit ripen. Today's word.
Your line: the blacksmith endured. Today, take on one small discomfort for someone else's good, and don't mention it. Day eight hundred fifty-four.
